title: Evaluating Non‐Native Piscivorous Fish Removal in a Large Water Diversion Forebay: A Synthesis of Piscivore Catch Rates, Prey Survival, and Bioenergetics Modeling
content:
ABSTRACT

We evaluated whether sustained removal of non-native piscivorous fish—Striped Bass (Morone saxatilis), black bass (Micropterus spp.), and catfish (Ictaluridae)—altered piscivore catch rates and improved survival of juvenile Chinook Salmon (Oncorhynchus tshawytscha) and Central Valley Steelhead (O. mykiss) within an 8.9-km2 water diversion forebay where predation by non-native fish contributes low juvenile salmonid survival. Despite removing 113,072 fish over 8 years, we found no evidence that removals at this scale consistently reduced predator catch rates or increased survival of tagged salmonids. Post hoc bioenergetics modeling indicated that Striped Bass removals alone would rarely meet the regulatory requirement that the juvenile salmonid mortality rate during forebay passage not exceed 40%. Where achievable, mean annual removal effort would need to be at least four times greater than that implemented. These results indicate that meeting the regulatory requirement necessitates substantially greater removal effort implemented as part of an integrated predator management strategy.
